name: Argentina
traditionNote: A codified civil-law system with a constitutional structure borrowed from the United States: the codes are federal and apply everywhere, but review of constitutionality is diffuse — any judge may refuse to apply a norm, and the ruling binds only that case.
summary: A statute (ley) is sanctioned by both chambers of Congress — the Cámara de Diputados and the Senado — promulgated by the Executive expressly or tacitly after ten working days, and published in the Boletín Oficial. Under Article 5 of the Civil and Commercial Code it takes effect on the eighth day after official publication unless it fixes its own date. Below statutes the Executive issues decretos reglamentarios, and ministries resoluciones and disposiciones, all published in the same gazette. Two instruments have no clean parallel elsewhere: the decreto de necesidad y urgencia, a decree with the force of law that Article 99(3) permits in exceptional circumstances, and delegated legislation under Article 76. Both go to a standing bicameral committee, and under the statute regulating them a DNU remains in force unless both chambers reject it — so silence sustains it. Argentina is federal: the provinces kept every power they did not delegate, each has its own constitution, legislature, courts and gazette, and the federal codes are applied by provincial judges rather than by federal ones.
hierarchy: Constitución Nacional (1853, with the reforms of 1860, 1866, 1898, 1957 and 1994) and the eleven human rights instruments given constitutional rank by Article 75(22)
Other treaties and concordats, which under Article 75(22) rank above ordinary statutes
Leyes nacionales — statutes of Congress, including the codes of substantive law
Decretos de necesidad y urgencia and delegated legislation, which have the force of statute within the limits of Articles 99(3) and 76
Decretos reglamentarios of the Executive, then ministerial resoluciones and agency disposiciones
Constituciones provinciales and provincial statutes, within the powers the provinces did not delegate
Ordenanzas municipales — municipal enactments under the autonomy guaranteed by Article 123

gazette.name: Boletin Oficial de la Republica Argentina
gazette.native: Boletín Oficial de la República Argentina (BORA)
gazette.en: Official Gazette of the Argentine Republic
gazette.authority: Secretaría Legal y Técnica de la Presidencia de la Nación
gazette.coverage: Published every working day since 1893, in four sections; the digital edition is served as a digitally signed PDF and the archive of past editions is open
gazette.desc: Where a federal norm is published and from which its entry into force is counted. The four sections sort what you are looking at: legislation and official notices in the first, company and judicial notices in the second, procurement in the third, internet domains in the fourth. Each daily edition is signed digitally and time-stamped on Blockchain Federal Argentina, so an edition can be verified rather than merely trusted.
gazette.howto: Open a section directly — /seccion/primera for legislation — or use 'Búsqueda avanzada' to search across editions by date, type of norm, issuing body and text. 'Ediciones Anteriores' reaches any past day, and the signature panel of the downloaded PDF is what proves the copy is the published one.
gazette.note: Publication starts the clock: the default under Article 5 of the Civil and Commercial Code is the eighth day after publication, and a great many norms displace it with a date of their own.

constitution.name: Constitucion de la Nacion Argentina
constitution.authority: Convención Constituyente; official text ordered published by Ley 24.430
constitution.coverage: The 1853 text with the reforms of 1860, 1866, 1898, 1957 and 1994, published as the official text under Ley 24.430 in the Boletín Oficial of 10 January 1995
constitution.desc: A constitution modelled on the United States and then, in 1994, given a rights architecture of its own: Article 75(22) grants constitutional rank to eleven named human rights instruments, so the American Convention and the UN covenants are read as part of the constitutional text rather than beside it. Article 43 adds amparo, habeas data and habeas corpus as express remedies.
constitution.howto: Read the official text through the Ministry of Justice's normative library, or in InfoLeg at the anexos address for Ley 24.430; the Senate publishes both the current text and the original 1853 text on its own site. Reform requires Congress to declare the need for it by two-thirds and a convention elected for the purpose.
constitution.note: Constitutional review is diffuse: any judge may declare a norm unconstitutional in the case before them, and the declaration binds only that case. There is no erga omnes annulment, and the Supreme Court's authority rests on the practice of following it rather than on a formal rule.

sources.name: Biblioteca de normativa (Argentina.gob.ar)
sources.authority: Ministerio de Justicia de la Nación — Infoleg
sources.coverage: Updated texts of statutes, decrees, resolutions and other norms, national and provincial, with links back to the Boletín Oficial edition that published each one
sources.desc: The modern face of InfoLeg, and the practical starting point: it offers the updated version of a norm rather than the text as published, and its jurisdiction selector reaches provincial legislation as well as federal — which no other single Argentine service does well.
sources.howto: Choose the jurisdiction (Nacional or Provincial) and the type of norm, then search by number, year or words in the title. A norm's page gives the updated text, the original text and the publication particulars — Boletín Oficial number, date and page.
sources.note: Updated texts are prepared editorially by the Ministry. Where wording is contested, the Boletín Oficial item is the published record.

sources.name: InfoLeg
sources.authority: Dirección Nacional del Sistema Argentino de Información Jurídica, Ministerio de Justicia
sources.coverage: National legislation from the nineteenth century onward, by type and number, with updated texts, original texts and the norms that amended each one
sources.desc: The older InfoLeg interface, still the fastest route when you have a citation. Its type list is a map of Argentine instrument names in itself — ley, decreto, decisión administrativa, resolución, disposición, acordada, laudo — and the distinctions between them carry real weight.
sources.howto: Search by type, number and year — leave the year blank for a ley, since statute numbers do not repeat — or by text and issuing dependency. Documents live at stable anexos addresses, which is why Argentine citations so often point at servicios.infoleg.gob.ar.
sources.note: Where a norm is missing, the site asks you to request it through its consultation form rather than assuming it does not exist.

sources.name: SAIJ
sources.authority: Ministerio de Justicia de la Nación
sources.coverage: Legislation national and provincial, case law from federal and provincial courts, doctrine, and the thesaurus of legal terms, released as open data
sources.desc: The broadest of the state's legal databases, and the one that reaches provincial case law — which is otherwise scattered across twenty-four judicial systems. It also publishes its holdings as open data, which is unusual in the region.
sources.howto: Search across legislación, jurisprudencia and doctrina, then narrow by jurisdiction; provincial coverage is uneven but is far better than nothing. The site sits behind a bot wall and answers automated requests with 403 while serving browsers normally.
sources.note: Case law here is a selection prepared from what the courts publish, not a complete record of judgments.

sources.name: Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nacion
sources.native: Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación
sources.authority: Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación
sources.coverage: The Court's decisions, its acordadas, the Fallos collection, statistics and the judicial information centre's coverage of the federal courts
sources.desc: The apex of a diffuse system: it reaches most cases through the recurso extraordinario federal, and its own doctrine of arbitrariedad de sentencia is what lets it review decisions that would otherwise be outside its jurisdiction. Its acordadas regulate the working of the whole federal judiciary.
sources.howto: Decisions are cited from the Fallos collection as volume and page — Fallos: 340:1554 — and the Court's site carries the collection, the acordadas and its news of the federal courts. For searching by subject rather than citation, use the jurisprudence services below.
sources.note: A declaration of unconstitutionality binds only the parties. The Court can and does reverse itself, so the date of a Fallos citation matters as much as its content.

sources.name: Jurisprudencia de la CSJN
sources.authority: Secretaría de Jurisprudencia, Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación
sources.coverage: The Court's own jurisprudence service, with thematic collections, leading-case compilations and the summaries service
sources.desc: The Court's curated view of its own case law, organised by subject rather than by date — which is how Argentine practitioners actually approach a line of Fallos.
sources.howto: Work from the thematic collections for an overview of a line of decisions, then move to the summaries search for individual holdings; both link back to the full text of the judgment.
sources.note: Summaries are editorial notes prepared by the Court's secretariat, not part of the judgment.

sources.name: Sumarios de la CSJN
sources.authority: Secretaría de Jurisprudencia, Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación
sources.coverage: Summaries of Supreme Court holdings from 1863 to the present, searchable by text, subject voces, case name, date and Fallos volume and page
sources.desc: A century and a half of Supreme Court holdings in one index. The voces — the controlled subject terms — are the key to it: Argentine research proceeds by voz far more than by keyword, and the same voz will pull a line of cases across decades.
sources.howto: Search by exact phrase, all words or nearby words, or by voces, autos and date range; if you already have a citation, the Tomo and Página fields resolve it directly. Each summary links to the judgment it came from.
sources.note: Coverage back to 1863 is of summaries, not full texts; older judgments in full are in the printed Fallos volumes.

sources.name: Poder Judicial de la Nacion
sources.authority: Consejo de la Magistratura and the federal courts
sources.coverage: Case tracking across the national and federal courts, court lists, electronic filing and the public consultation of proceedings
sources.desc: The working system of the federal courts. Its consulta de causas is where a case is followed by number, and it is often the only public sight of a first-instance proceeding, since the great majority of Argentine judgments are never published anywhere.
sources.howto: Use the case consultation with the case number and the court, or search by party where the system allows it; the notification service publishes the daily list for each court. Provincial courts run their own systems entirely separately.
sources.note: A case file's public view is limited and does not reproduce the judgment in every instance; the judgment itself may be reachable only through the court's own publication.

sources.name: Senado de la Nacion
sources.native: Honorable Senado de la Nación Argentina
sources.coverage: Bills and their file histories, committee opinions (dictámenes), sitting records and votes, plus the constitutional texts the chamber publishes
sources.desc: The Senate's parliamentary information service, and the more reliable half of Congress online. A bill's file shows the dictamen de comisión — the committee opinion — which is the Argentine equivalent of a legislative report and the usual evidence of what a provision was meant to do.
sources.howto: Search bills by number and year or by subject, then follow the file through committee and both chambers; the Senate also publishes the current constitutional text and the original 1853 text under its institutional section.
sources.note: The Chamber of Deputies runs its own parliamentary system, which is frequently unreachable from outside Argentina; where it is, the Senate file usually records the Chamber's stages as well.

sources.name: Biblioteca Digital de Tratados
sources.authority: Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores, Comercio Internacional y Culto
sources.coverage: Bilateral and multilateral treaties to which Argentina is or has been a party, with their texts, approving statutes and status
sources.desc: Treaties matter more in Argentine law than in most: Article 75(22) puts them above ordinary statutes, and gives eleven human rights instruments the same rank as the Constitution itself. This is the state's record of what has been signed, approved and brought into force.
sources.howto: Search by counterpart, subject or date; each record gives the approving ley and the instrument's status. The approving statute is itself a norm in InfoLeg, and it is the one that shows any reservation Argentina made.
sources.note: Approval by Congress is not the same as entry into force; check the status field before treating a treaty as binding.

sources.name: Red de Boletines Oficiales
sources.native: Red de Boletines Oficiales de la República Argentina
sources.authority: The national gazette together with the provincial gazettes
sources.coverage: The official gazettes of the twenty-three provinces and the City of Buenos Aires, with links to each
sources.desc: Argentina has twenty-five gazettes, not one. A provincial statute is published in that province's Boletín Oficial and nowhere else, so the national gazette is only the federal slice — this network is the state's own index of the rest.
sources.howto: Pick the province and follow into its gazette, each of which has its own search, formats and archive depth. Some provincial gazettes are unreachable from outside Argentina and some charge for access to older editions.
sources.note: A directory rather than a database: nothing is searchable across provinces from here, and the Ministry of Justice's normative library is usually the better first try for a provincial statute.

sources.name: Boletin Oficial de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires
sources.native: Boletín Oficial de la Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires
sources.en: Official Gazette of the City of Buenos Aires
sources.authority: Gobierno de la Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires
sources.coverage: The City's daily gazette with its normative archive, searchable by date, type and issuing body
sources.desc: Shown as the pattern for the subnational tier, and a special case in its own right: since the 1994 reform the City has been autonomous, with its own constitution, legislature and judiciary, so its leyes are city statutes rather than municipal ordinances.
sources.howto: Open the day's edition or search the normative archive by number, year and type; the City's own consolidated normative system is linked from the same site.
sources.note: City law applies only in the Autonomous City. The surrounding Province of Buenos Aires is a separate jurisdiction with a separate gazette.

sources.name: Derecho Facil
sources.authority: Ministerio de Justicia de la Nación
sources.coverage: Plain-language accounts of statutes and of everyday legal situations, with links to the norms behind them
sources.desc: The Ministry's plain-language service: what a statute does, written for the people it applies to. It covers a limited set of subjects and is honest on its own pages that some sections are out of date.
sources.howto: Browse 'Ley Simple' for a statute or 'Situaciones' for a practical problem; each entry links to the norm itself, which is what governs.
sources.note: Explanations, not law. Where the plain-language version and the norm differ, the norm governs.

sources.name: Ministerio Publico Fiscal
sources.native: Ministerio Público Fiscal de la Nación
sources.coverage: Opinions of the Procurador General before the Supreme Court, prosecution guidelines and resolutions, and the specialised units' reports
sources.desc: The dictámenes of the Procurador General are filed before the Supreme Court decides, and are often the fullest analysis available of the question the Court is about to answer — frequently cited, and sometimes adopted wholesale in the Court's judgment.
sources.howto: Search the dictámenes by case name or subject, and the resoluciones for the guidelines that bind federal prosecutors; both are indexed by year.
sources.note: An opinion binds nobody. Its weight is that the Court reads it first and often follows it.

sources.name: Defensor del Pueblo de la Nacion
sources.native: Defensoría del Pueblo de la Nación
sources.authority: Defensoría del Pueblo de la Nación, an independent body under Article 86 of the Constitution
sources.coverage: Recommendations, resolutions and annual reports on administrative conduct and the protection of rights
sources.desc: A constitutional office with standing to bring actions in defence of collective rights — which in Argentina, where the amparo colectivo does much of the work of public interest litigation, makes its files a useful trace of disputes that later reach the courts.
sources.howto: Browse the recommendations and annual reports by subject and year; each states the body complained of and the provisions at issue.
sources.note: The office has spent long periods vacant, so the absence of recent material may reflect that rather than a lack of complaints.

sources.name: datos.gob.ar
sources.native: datos.gob.ar — Portal Nacional de Datos Abiertos
sources.coverage: Public sector datasets, including legislative, judicial and gazette-derived data published by ministries and agencies
sources.desc: Where structured legal and judicial data is published when it is published at all — the gazette and the legislation services offer no public API of their own, so bulk work generally starts here.
sources.howto: Search the catalogue by publisher or subject; each dataset names the responsible body, its format and its update frequency.
sources.note: Datasets, not legal texts. Nothing here is a source of law.

sources.name: Mercosur
sources.coverage: The founding treaties and protocols and the decisions, resolutions and directives of the bloc's organs, with their incorporation status for each member state
sources.desc: Argentina is a founding member, and Mercosur norms are not directly applicable: most require incorporation into Argentine law, usually by decree or resolution, before they bind anyone. The bloc's database records whether Argentina has incorporated a given norm and by which instrument.
sources.howto: Find the norm by organ, year and number, check its incorporation status for Argentina, and follow to the Argentine instrument that incorporated it — that instrument, published in the Boletín Oficial, is what binds domestically.
sources.note: The site answers automated requests with 403 while serving browsers normally. Disputes go to ad hoc arbitral tribunals and the Tribunal Permanente de Revisión, not to a court with direct effect.

findLaw.task: Find the current text of a statute
findLaw.steps: Search the Ministry of Justice's normative library by number and year and open the updated text; statute numbers do not repeat, so 'ley 26994' is unambiguous. The page also gives the original text and the Boletín Oficial edition that published it.

findLaw.task: Read the norm exactly as published
findLaw.steps: Take the Boletín Oficial date and section from the norm's record and open that edition, or use the advanced search across editions. The daily PDF is digitally signed and time-stamped, so the signature panel is what tells you the copy is authentic.
findLaw.source: Boletín Oficial de la República Argentina

findLaw.task: Work out when a rule starts to apply
findLaw.steps: Read the final articles of the norm. If it fixes no date, Article 5 of the Civil and Commercial Code applies: it takes effect on the eighth day after official publication. For a decreto de necesidad y urgencia, check also whether the bicameral committee and the chambers have dealt with it — it stays in force unless both chambers reject it.

If you have a Fallos citation, enter the volume and page in the summaries search. If you have a subject, search by voces — the controlled terms are how Argentine case-law research is done — and follow the summary through to the full judgment.

findLaw.task: Check whether a provision has been held unconstitutional
findLaw.steps: There is no register of struck-down norms, because nothing is struck down for everyone: review is diffuse and a declaration binds only the parties. Search the Supreme Court's holdings for the provision and read the line of cases, then check whether Congress has since amended the norm — the provision itself stays in the books either way.

Try the normative library first with the jurisdiction set to Provincial, then go to the province's own gazette through the network of official gazettes. For the Autonomous City of Buenos Aires, use the City's gazette — its leyes are city statutes, not municipal ordinances, and the surrounding province is a separate jurisdiction.
findLaw.source: Red de Boletines Oficiales / Boletín Oficial CABA

findLaw.task: Follow a bill, or read why a statute was written
findLaw.steps: Open the bill's file in the Senate's parliamentary system and read the dictamen de comisión and the sitting records; the fundamentos attached to the original bill state its purpose. Where the Chamber of Deputies' own system is unreachable, the Senate file usually records both chambers' stages.
findLaw.source: Senado de la Nación — información parlamentaria

subnational: Argentina is a federation of twenty-three provinces and the Autonomous City of Buenos Aires, and Article 121 leaves the provinces every power they did not delegate to the federal government. Each has its own constitution, legislature, courts and Boletín Oficial, and a provincial statute is published in that provincial gazette and nowhere else — there are twenty-five gazettes in all, indexed by the Red de Boletines Oficiales. The division is not the usual federal one: under Article 75(12) the substantive codes — civil and commercial, criminal, labour, mining — are enacted by the national Congress and apply throughout the country, but they are applied by provincial courts, while procedure is provincial, so the same code is litigated under twenty-four different procedural regimes. The City of Buenos Aires became autonomous in 1994 with its own constitution and judiciary, and its enactments are leyes rather than ordinances. Below the provinces, municipalities have the autonomy guaranteed by Article 123 in the terms each provincial constitution sets, and issue ordenanzas published locally, which are largely absent from any national database.
caveats: Nothing in Argentina is struck down for everyone: review of constitutionality is diffuse, a declaration binds only the parties, and a provision repeatedly held unconstitutional remains in force until Congress repeals it. The updated texts in the Ministry of Justice's services are editorial work over what the gazette published, and the Boletín Oficial item is the record — one reason the daily edition is digitally signed and time-stamped. Decrees of necessity and urgency deserve particular care: they have the force of statute from publication and remain in force unless both chambers reject them, so a norm can be operative for years without ever having been approved by Congress. Federal law is only part of the answer, since twenty-four other jurisdictions legislate and publish separately, several of their gazettes are unreachable from outside the country, and municipal ordinances are usually not online at all. Case-law publication is thin below the Supreme Court: most judgments are never published, and what SAIJ and the courts do publish is a selection. Nothing is translated — Argentine law exists in Spanish only.
